summary: This informational memo describes how ICPv2 from RFC 2186 is applied to web caching.

plainLanguage.summary: ICP lets one web cache ask a neighbour whether it already has a page, before going to the original server. The memo describes how caches are arranged in parent and sibling relationships, how a cache decides which neighbour to ask, and the security problems of a protocol with no authentication.

questions: how to use icp with web caches
what is icp internet cache protocol
what is the difference between a parent and sibling cache
subtitle: How web caches ask each other whether they already hold a page, and what that costs.

tldr.problem: A cache that does not hold a page has to fetch it from somewhere, and the origin server is often further away than a neighbouring cache.
tldr.mechanism: ICP is a small message format that caches exchange to ask whether a neighbouring cache holds a URL. Each cache compares the answers with its own configuration, which says which peers are parents and which are siblings.
tldr.outcome: The protocol has no authentication and runs over UDP, so the memo lists the ways it can be attacked and the rules that limit the damage. It also records the design flaws of ICPv2 for anyone writing the next version.

today: RFC 2187 is an Informational memo from September 1997, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes how the Harvest and Squid caches implemented ICP, and it is explicit that some of the practices it records are suboptimal and exist for historical reasons.

sections.title: Introduction and Why ICP Is Used
sections.content:
ICP is a lightweight message format used for communicating among Web caches. It is used to exchange hints about the existence of URLs in neighbour caches, and caches exchange ICP queries and replies to gather information for use in selecting the most appropriate location from which to retrieve an object. This memo describes the application of ICP version 2 to Web caching: the companion document RFC 2186 describes the format and syntax of the protocol itself, while this one focuses on deployment, efficiency, security and interaction with other aspects of Web traffic behaviour.

The memo is deliberately descriptive rather than prescriptive. It avoids making judgements about whether or how ICP should be used in particular Web caching configurations, because ICP may be a net win in some situations and a net loss in others. Certain practices described are acknowledged to be suboptimal: some exist for historical reasons, and some aspects have been improved in later versions. Since the document serves only to describe current practices, the authors focus on documenting rather than evaluating, while still addressing known security problems and other shortcomings.

Without ICP or something similar, sibling relationships between caches cannot exist, because those depend on a way to ask nearby caches about a document. One concern is the delay that a query and reply adds to an HTTP transaction, but if the query finds the object in a nearby cache, the delay may be more than offset by the faster delivery of the data. The caches and the protocol are both designed to return ICP requests quickly, and the application does minimal processing, so most of the delay is transmission on the network. ICP also reports whether a neighbour is reachable: if replies stop arriving, either the network path is congested or down, or the neighbour's cache application is not running, and in either case the cache should not use that neighbour at the time. And because an idle cache can turn replies around faster than a busy one, ICP provides some form of load balancing.

ICP was initially developed by Peter Danzig and others at the University of Southern California as a central part of hierarchical caching in the Harvest research project.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of asking a neighbour is speed. A page held one hop away comes back faster than the same page fetched from the server that published it.

sections.title: Web Cache Hierarchies and How Peers Are Set Up
sections.content:
A single Web cache reduces the traffic generated by the clients behind it, and a group of caches can benefit by sharing another cache in much the same way. The Harvest researchers saw that it would be important to connect Web caches hierarchically. In a cache hierarchy, or mesh, one cache establishes peering relationships with its neighbour caches, and there are two types of relationship: parent and sibling. A parent cache is essentially one level up in the hierarchy, and a sibling cache is on the same level. The terms neighbour and peer are used for either, when they are a single cache-hop away.

The general flow of document requests is up the hierarchy. When a cache does not hold a requested object, it may ask via ICP whether any of its neighbour caches has it. If one does, that is a neighbour hit, and the cache requests the object from there. If none does, that is a neighbour miss, and the cache must forward the request either to a parent or directly to the origin server. The essential difference between a parent and a sibling is that a neighbour hit may be fetched from either, but a neighbour miss may not be fetched from a sibling: in a sibling relationship the cache can only ask to retrieve objects the sibling already has cached, while the same cache can ask a parent to retrieve any object whether or not it is cached. A parent cache's role is to provide transit for the request if necessary, and parent caches are ideally located within or on the way to a transit Internet service provider.

Both Squid and Harvest allow complex hierarchical configurations. One cache can be specified to be used for only a certain class of requests, such as URLs from a specific DNS domain, and it is even possible to treat a neighbour as a sibling for some requests and as a parent for others. The model also includes features to prevent top-level caches from becoming choke points: the ability to restrict parents by domain, and the rule that a cache only forwards cacheable requests to its neighbours. A large class of Web requests is inherently uncacheable, including requests requiring certain types of authentication, session-encrypted data, highly personalized responses and certain types of database queries, and lower level caches should handle these requests directly rather than burdening parent caches.

Configuring caches within a hierarchy requires establishing peering relationships, which currently involves manual configuration at both peering endpoints: one cache must indicate that the other is a parent or sibling, and the other will most likely have to add the first cache to its access control lists. On the cache that sends queries, peers are declared with a directive of the form cache_host hostname type http-port icp-port [options], where the type is parent, sibling or multicast. On the cache that receives the queries, the relationship is governed by access lists similar to those used for routing peers, and if there are no access lines present the cache allows the request by default. The access control entries regulate the relationships between the caches; the type of relationship is not encoded in the ICP query itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A parent cache will go and fetch anything for you, even something it does not hold yet. A sibling cache only hands over what it already has. That single difference decides who can be asked for a miss.

sections.title: Applying the Protocol
sections.content:
The basic sequence of events in an ICP transaction is that a local cache receives an HTTP request from a cache client, sends ICP queries, the peer caches receive the queries and send ICP replies, and the local cache receives the replies and decides where to forward the request.

Not every HTTP request produces an ICP query. A cache hit needs no ICP because the request is satisfied immediately. For origin servers very close to the cache, the administrator says what counts as local with the local_domain and local_ip configuration options, and the cache always contacts a local server directly. Other classes of request may also be forwarded directly, such as all non-GET request methods, and a cache can be configured not to use peers for URLs matching a hierarchy stoplist. For an HTTP request to yield an ICP transaction it must not be a cache hit, must not be to a local server, must be a GET request, and must not match the hierarchy stoplist. The memo calls this a hierarchical request.

By default a cache sends an ICP_OP_QUERY message to each peer, unless restrictions prevent it: a directive called cache_host_domain can restrict which DNS domains a peer is asked about, a sibling is not asked when the request carries a Pragma: no-cache header because the sibling would be asked to transit the request, and a peer can be configured never to be sent ICP queries. The cache calculates how many replies to expect, normally one per query, except when the peer is believed to be down or when sending to a multicast address. Because ICP uses UDP, queries and replies may be dropped by the network, so the cache installs a timeout event; Squid and Harvest use a two second timeout by default, and if object retrieval has not started when it fires, a source is selected instead.

On receiving a query, a cache decides which reply to send, testing the opcodes in order. If the URL cannot be parsed the reply is ICP_OP_ERR. If the access controls do not allow the peer, the reply is ICP_OP_DENIED, and if more than 95% of more than 100 replies to that peer have been denied then no reply is sent at all, which stops misconfigured caches sending messages back and forth endlessly. Otherwise the cache checks whether it holds the URL and, if the cached entry is fresh for at least the next 30 seconds, it can reply ICP_OP_HIT, or ICP_OP_HIT_OBJ if the query asked for it and the whole object plus URL fits in an ICP message, whose maximum size is 16 Kbytes. Failing that, the cache replies ICP_OP_MISS_NOFETCH if it does not want the peer to fetch the object from it, and ICP_OP_MISS by default, which, when the replying cache is a parent, is an invitation to fetch the URL through it.

On the querying side, some replies are ignored: those from an unknown peer, those naming an object that does not exist, and those for an object already being fetched. An ICP_OP_HIT starts the retrieval at once, and an ICP_OP_HIT_OBJ carries the object with it. An ICP_OP_SECHO starts the retrieval from the origin server, because it arrived before any hit. An ICP_OP_MISS from a sibling is ignored, while a miss from a parent is remembered, either the first parent to miss or the parent with the lowest round-trip time to the origin. When all peers miss, the cache waits for the expected number of replies or for the timeout, and then forwards the request to the peer with the lowest round-trip time, to the first parent to miss, or straight to the origin server.
sections.plainLanguage: The cache sends out its questions, waits for the answers, and picks a source. If nothing useful comes back, it falls back on the parent or the original server.

sections.title: Firewalls and Multicast
sections.content:
Operating a Web cache behind a firewall or in a private network poses some problems, and the hard part is working out whether the cache is able to connect to the origin server. Harvest and Squid provide an inside_firewall directive to list DNS domains on the near side of a firewall, and everything else is assumed to be on the far side; Squid also has a firewall_ip directive so that inside hosts can be named by IP address. In a simple configuration a Squid cache behind a firewall has only one parent cache, which is on the firewall itself, and it must use that parent for all servers beyond the firewall, so there is no need to use ICP at all. In a more complex configuration there may be several peer caches also behind the firewall, and here ICP may be used to check for cache hits among them. If no replies come back, the cache cannot forward straight to the origin server and must pick a parent cache, either at random or from configuration information.

For efficient distribution a cache may deliver ICP queries to a multicast address, and neighbour caches may join the multicast group to receive them. Current practice is that caches send ICP replies only to unicast addresses, for three reasons: multicasting replies would not reduce the number of packets sent, it prevents other group members from receiving unexpected replies, and the reply should follow unicast routing paths to show that unicast connectivity exists between the receiver and the sender, since the later HTTP request will be unicast routed.

Trust is an important part of inter-cache relationships. A cache should not automatically trust a cache which replies to a multicast ICP query, and should ignore ICP messages from addresses that are not configured as neighbours, or one could pollute a cache mesh by running an illegitimate cache, having it join the group, return ICP_OP_HIT for every request and then deliver bogus content. Cache administrators must use the minimum multicast TTL required to reach all group members, since joining a multicast group requires no special privileges and there is no way to stop anyone from joining your group. Two groups using the same multicast address could overlap, which would cause a cache to receive replies from unknown neighbours that it must always ignore, and the memo recommends limiting the scope of queries with appropriate TTLs, using a tool such as mtrace to determine them.

Because there is no way to know how many replies a multicast query will produce, Squid regularly sends test queries to the group peers only, every 15 minutes, installs a timeout event and counts the replies until it fires. The received count varies considerably, so the number of replies to expect is calculated as a moving average, rounded down to the nearest integer.
sections.plainLanguage: A cache behind a firewall cannot always reach the original server, so it has to have a parent to fall back on. And when queries go out to a multicast group, a cache must be careful about who it believes.

sections.title: Lessons Learned
sections.content:
ICP is notably different from HTTP. HTTP supports a rich and sophisticated set of features, whereas ICP was designed to be simple, small and efficient. HTTP request and reply headers consist of lines of ASCII text delimited by a CRLF pair, while ICP uses a fixed size header and represents numbers in binary; the only thing the two have in common is the URL. The ICP message does not even include the HTTP request method, because the original implementation assumed that only GET requests would be cacheable and that there would be no need to locate non-GET requests in neighbour caches.

HTTP defines features that matter for caching but cannot be expressed with the current ICP protocol: Pragma: no-cache, If-Modified-Since and the Cache-Control features of HTTP/1.1. An ICP_OP_HIT_OBJ message may deliver an object which does not obey all of the request header constraints, and these differences are the reason the authors discourage the use of the ICP_OP_HIT_OBJ feature. The ICP message also has no field saying what the relationship between the two caches is. A sibling cache can only respond with HIT or MISS, not with an instruction about whether the object may be fetched from it, so the querying cache must apply the reply to its own configuration to prevent it from resolving misses through a sibling. The memo calls this constraint awkward, because the relationship can be configured only in the cache originating the requests, and indirectly through the access controls on the queried cache.

The role of ICP is also changing. One understanding is that its role is only object location, providing hints about whether a named object exists in a neighbour cache, on the assumption that cache hits are highly desirable. If an ICP message is lost, nothing significant is lost, because the request will be satisfied anyway. ICP is increasingly being tasked with a more complex role, conveying cache usage policy: for example a border cache that will serve any object already in its cache and any object from its own servers, but will not provide transit for requests where neither the client nor the server falls within its domain. To convey policy the ICP exchange must very accurately predict the result of a later HTTP request, but that result often depends on other request fields such as Cache-Control, so it is not possible for ICP to predict it accurately without more, or perhaps all, of the HTTP request.

The authors also record the design flaws of ICPv2 so that a future version can avoid them. The NULL-terminated URL in the payload field forces a receiver to step through the message an octet at a time to find some fields. Two fields, the Sender Host Address and the Requester Host Address, are IPv4 specific, though neither is used in practice and they are normally zero-filled; if IP addresses do have a role, there needs to be an address family descriptor for each. Options are limited to 32 option flags and 32 bits of option data, which should be more like TCP, with an option descriptor followed by option data. The URL string, though used as the cache key, no longer serves that role adequately, since some HTTP responses now vary according to the requestor's User-Agent and other headers, and a cache key must incorporate all non-transport headers present in the client's request. ICPv2 uses different opcode values for queries and responses, and includes no authentication fields at all.
sections.plainLanguage: ICP was built to be small, and that shows. It cannot carry everything HTTP can, so it is being pushed further than it was designed for.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security is an issue with ICP over UDP because of its connectionless nature. The first line of defence is to check the source IP address of the ICP message. ICP query messages should be processed if the access control rules allow the querying address access to the cache, but ICP reply messages must only be accepted from known neighbours, and a cache must ignore replies from unknown addresses. Because the validity of an address in an IP packet is trusted, ICP is susceptible to IP address spoofing, though the IP Authentication Header can be used underneath ICP to provide cryptographic authentication of the whole IP packet and so remove the risk.

The memo then works through the attacks. Inserting bogus replies can prevent a neighbour from being used, for instance by sending an ICP_OP_MISS_NOFETCH before the real reply or by blasting the cache with ICP_OP_DENIED messages until the threshold is reached; it can force a neighbour to be used, by sending an ICP_OP_HIT or an ICP_OP_SECHO before the real reply; and it can poison the cache, since ICP_OP_HIT_OBJ carries actual object data. Eavesdropping is easy when queries are multicast, and the eavesdropper can obtain a list of the URLs being browsed, though the Requestor Host Address is zero-filled by Squid and Harvest so the URLs cannot be mapped back to individual host systems. Squid and Harvest do not by default send ICP messages for URLs containing cgi-bin or ?, because those URLs sometimes carry sensitive information as argument parameters.

Blocking ICP messages looks like link failure or congestion, prevents the use of a neighbour, and if every message is blocked the cache removes the neighbour from its selection algorithm. Delaying messages adds delay to the later HTTP request, and messages delayed past the timeout behave as if they had been blocked. A denial of service attack, where the ICP port is flooded with a continuous stream of bogus messages, has three weaknesses: the application may log every bogus message and fill up a disk partition, the socket receive queue may fill so that legitimate messages are dropped, and the host may waste processor cycles receiving the bogus messages.

Altering fields of a reply matters in different ways. Changing the opcode is much like inserting a bogus message. Altering the version field may have unpredictable consequences if the new number is recognized and supported, and both version numbers 2 and 3 were in use at the time of writing. An incorrect message length should be detected as an invalid ICP message. Altering the request number or the URL causes the cache key lookup to fail, so the reply is ignored, which is like blocking it altogether. The option bitfields carry little risk, because any option bit set in a reply that was not set in the query is detectable and the message must be ignored, while clearing a bit is allowed; but ICP_FLAG_SRC_RTT is the only option that uses the option data field, and altering the round-trip time values there can affect which neighbour is chosen.

The memo's summary is that ICP_OP_HIT_OBJ is particularly vulnerable because it includes object data, and its use is discouraged. Falsifying, altering, inserting or blocking ICP messages can cause an HTTP request to fail only in two situations: when the cache is behind a firewall and cannot connect directly to the origin server, and when a false ICP_OP_HIT reply causes the request to be forwarded to a sibling where the request is a cache miss and the sibling refuses to continue forwarding on behalf of the originating cache. They can easily cause requests to be forwarded, or not forwarded, to certain neighbours; if the neighbour cache has also been compromised, it could serve bogus content and pollute a cache hierarchy. Blocking or delaying ICP messages can cause the HTTP request to be further delayed, but still satisfied.
sections.plainLanguage: ICP trusts the sender's address and carries no authentication of its own, so anyone who can reach the port can lie about what a cache holds.

viz.caption: THE ICP REPLY OPCODES, IN THE ORDER THEY ARE TESTED

items.label: Error
items.desc: The URL in the payload could not be parsed.

items.label: Denied
items.desc: The access controls do not allow the peer to make this request.

items.label: Hit
items.desc: The object is held here and is fresh for at least the next 30 seconds.

items.label: Hit with object
items.desc: The reply carries the object itself, if it fits in the 16 Kbyte message.

items.label: Miss, do not fetch
items.desc: The object is not here, and the peer should not fetch it from here.

items.label: Miss
items.desc: The object is not here; from a parent, an invitation to fetch it through this cache.
